# Mahājanakajātaka (Ja 539)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahājanakajātaka* (Ja 539), translated as *The Longer Tale of King Janaka*, is one of the renowned final ten "great stories" (*mahājātakas*) of the canonical Pali Jātaka collection [Appleton 2010; Wood 2005; SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related this story of the past while residing at Jetavana to illustrate his own Great Renunciation [SuttaCentral]. Set in a cosmic era when the human lifespan was 10,000 years, the narrative recounts the life of King Janaka (the Bodhisatta), who is shipwrecked, endures severe maritime trials, and reclaims his kingdom, embodying the perfection of energy (*viriya-pāramitā*) [Appleton 2010; Endo 1997]. The climax depicts Mahājanaka's dramatic departure from his palace into the forest to embrace ascetic life, successfully resisting the tearful entreaties of his subjects and his estranged wife, Queen Sīvalī [Murphy; Wood 2005].
SuttaCentral notes verse- and passage-level parallels across the Pali Canon, including the *Theragāthā* (Thag 1.97, 16.7), *Dhammapada* (Dhp 200), *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (SN 4.18), and other Jātakas (*Sarabhamigajātaka*, Ja 483; *Mahāsīlavajātaka*, Ja 51) [SuttaCentral]. Non-Pali parallels include the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, Patna Dharmapada, Udānavarga recensions (UV 30, UVS 30, and Chinese parallels T 210, T 212, T 213), and the *Mahābhārata* (12.268.4), alongside narrative parallels in the Jain *Uttarādhyayanasūtra* (chapter 9) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies 512 Pali text-reuse matches across 13 texts, predominantly with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as shared gāthās in the *Vessantarajātaka* (Ja 547), *Soṇakajātaka* (Ja 529), and *Todeyyattheraapadāna* (Tha-Ap 410) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments are registered with Sanskrit Vinaya and Mahāyāna texts (including the *Bhikṣuṇīvinaya*, *Lalitavistara*, and Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā*), as well as Tibetan translations of the *Udānavarga* and Kṣemendra's *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* [DharmaNexus].
The story is widely celebrated in Southeast Asian and Indian visual art, including early stone coping reliefs [Wood 2005], Cave 1 murals at Ajanta depicting royal courtly splendor and shipwreck scenes [Brancaccio 2010; Silk 1994], 8th–9th century Dvaravati boundary markers (*sīmā*) in Thailand [Murphy], and modern Thai temple murals [Appleton 2010]. In literature, it was famously adapted into a standard Burmese prose version by the monk Awbatha [Ray 1946], translated into English by James Gray from Burmese manuscripts [Bendall], and refashioned in 1996 by King Bhumibol Adulyadej of Thailand (*The Story of Mahajanaka*) to emphasize royal education and public governance rather than world-renouncing asceticism [Jory 2016].
